transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess I’m here because things have gotten a little... too full. I’ve been saying yes to everything—new art projects, workshops, fixing up the studio, calls with clients—and at first it felt exciting, like I could finally get everything moving.  

But now I’ve got deadlines stacked on deadlines, and the mortgage is sitting there in the back of my mind. I was even thinking about repainting the studio shelves, which is ridiculous because I haven’t finished the pieces that are actually due. So, yes, I think I’ve taken on more than I can realistically manage.
Have you been needing less sleep than usual?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, my sleep has never been perfectly tidy—especially when I’m working on a piece, because time sort of slips. I’ll think, “just one more layer,” and then I’m cleaning brushes at some strange hour. But needing less sleep… I don’t know if I’d put it that way. I haven’t really been tracking it.
Have you been feeling unusually high or euphoric lately?

Yes… I think so. Most days I’ve felt sort of buoyant, like lit up from the inside, like the studio and the garden were finally talking to each other—if that makes sense. I’d walk in and see three different things that needed doing and think, “Of course, yes, I can make all of this work.”

But then if someone asked, very reasonably, about invoices or whether I’d actually planned the time for it, I could get… sharp. Sharper than I meant to. It felt like they were poking holes in something beautiful before it even had a chance.
Have you been more active than usual, starting lots of new projects or tasks?

Yes, definitely more active. I’ve had this sort of humming current in me from morning on, like if I sat down it would just build up under my skin. So I kept finding things to do—rearranging the studio, drafting proposals, emailing people, fussing with supplies.

And the supplies thing is silly because I have drawers of things already, but then I start thinking the charcoal should be closer to the paper, and then I notice the shelves, and then I’m halfway into reorganizing everything instead of just… being still. Sitting quietly has felt almost impossible.
Lately, have you felt unusually confident or more capable than you normally are?

Yes… yes, I think so. Not just “I’m having a good workday” confident, but like—this sudden certainty that my illustration work could do something much bigger.

I kept thinking scientific journals have been missing a visual language for years, decades even, and that somehow I could be the one to finally make it clear for them. Which sounds grand when I say it out loud. I know that. But at the time it felt obvious, like when you find the right green for a leaf and then the whole painting stops arguing with you.
Have you been talking more than usual lately?

Yes… I think I have. In meetings especially, I’d hear myself speeding up, just going and going about layouts and pigments and symbols and then somehow budgets too—because of course the budget affects the paper, and the paper affects the whole feeling of the thing.

And then I’d notice people looking like they were waiting for a doorway into the conversation, but I wasn’t really leaving one. A couple of times they had to interrupt me just to answer, which felt rude for half a second, and then I realized, no, I’d been sort of… filling all the air.
Have you felt unusually driven to accomplish things lately?

Yes, very driven. That’s actually part of why I came in, because I keep saying yes to things—new client calls, workshops I suddenly think I should offer, improvements to the studio, proposals that need sketches and follow-up and all of it.

And then I’ll think, well, if I just fix the lighting over the drafting table, that will make everything smoother, but then that turns into moving shelves, and then I’m ordering storage boxes instead of finishing the actual work. My friend once said artists can make “preparing to work” into its own career, which is funny, but it’s not feeling that funny now.

I’ve taken on more than I can realistically manage, I think. The deadlines are starting to bunch up, and the mortgage is there in the background like this heavy thing, and I still keep acting like I can just push harder and somehow make it all fit.
Has this period caused serious problems in your life or work?

Yes… I mean, I keep wanting to say “not serious-serious,” because the studio is still standing and I’m still answering emails, but that’s not really honest.

My illustration deadlines have slipped. A few colleagues have started checking in on me, not in the usual friendly way, more like they’re trying to see if I’m still keeping track of things. And I hate that, because I’ve always been the person who notices the tiny details, like whether a shadow edge is too hard or if the label spacing is off.

And financially… yes, there’s a problem. I overcommitted, and I spent money I really should have kept aside to keep the studio secure. Now the mortgage feels… at risk, or close enough that I can’t pretend it isn’t. I keep thinking I can fix it with the next project, but the projects are exactly what I’m behind on.
Has there been a period like this that lasted at least one week without letting up?

Yes… definitely more than a week. It’s been more like three months, I think—since I took on the mortgage for the cottage-studio.

That was supposed to be such a good, grounding thing, you know, having a real space for the work. I remember thinking about the north light and where the big table would go, and then somehow everything just… kept accelerating from there. So yes, it hasn’t really let up.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

I’m not sure I can answer that neatly. I mean, I’ve had low stretches, of course—who hasn’t, especially when work gets strange or money is tight—but “most of the day nearly every day” for two weeks… I don’t know.

Sometimes I lose interest in starting something because it feels like the setup has become impossible, like the brushes need cleaning or the paper isn’t right, and then I remember this one teacher in graduate school who used to say artists are just professional avoiders with better vocabulary. But that’s not exactly the same as losing interest, is it?

So… I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear two-week block like that. Or at least I can’t point to one confidently.
Before this current stretch, have you ever had another period when you felt unusually energized or high like this?

I don’t really know. I’ve always had bursts, I guess—when a project catches fire and I stay with it longer than I meant to, or I get very excited about a color problem or a layout. But that feels… normal for me, or at least it used to.

Before this? I can’t point to another stretch and say, yes, that was the same thing. My memory sort of files everything by work deadlines and exhibitions, not by mood, which is probably inconvenient for your purposes. I remember one winter where I was making these tiny ink studies of window frames and got very obsessed with the spacing, but that’s not—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed another clear period like this before.
Before this current period, have you ever had another time when you felt this unusually energized or high?

Before this current period… I don’t think so, not in the same way. I mean, I’ve had times where I felt very buoyant, very lit up, like the studio and the garden were finally speaking to each other—honestly that sounds ridiculous when I say it, but that’s how it felt.

And then if someone questioned the plans, or asked about invoices, I could get sharp. Too sharp, probably. My sister once asked a perfectly ordinary question about expenses and I acted like she’d insulted the whole project. But that’s been mostly this recent stretch, not some earlier separate time I can clearly point to.
